opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the big practical bottlenecks right now. If you look at where the progress in vision-language-action models has come from, a lot of it comes from scale. These models inherit their backbones from large vision-language models with billions of parameters, and that's where much of the generalization and semantic understanding comes from. But a robot isn't a data center. On a legged robot or a humanoid you have a tight power budget, limited space, heat to dissipate, and you're running on a battery. Every watt the computer uses is a watt the actuators don't get, and it cuts into runtime.

Then there's latency. For high-level reasoning, like "go to the kitchen and pick up the cup," you can live with a few hundred milliseconds or even a second. But for control, especially dynamic locomotion or contact-rich manipulation, you need tens to hundreds of hertz, and you need it reliably. A big transformer on an embedded GPU just doesn't hit those rates at the model sizes we'd like. So people end up with hierarchical setups: a slow, large model that outputs some intermediate representation, and a fast, small policy underneath that tracks it. That works, but it's a compromise. The interface between the two levels becomes a design problem, and you lose some of the end-to-end benefit.

You could offload to the cloud, but then you depend on connectivity, and you get latency jitter, which is really bad for anything safety-critical. A robot that freezes because the Wi-Fi dropped isn't acceptable in a real deployment.

So right now there's a tension: the models that are most capable are too big to run onboard at control rates, and the ones that fit onboard lose a lot of what makes VLAs exciting. I think this will improve through better edge hardware, distillation, quantization, and smarter architectures that separate fast and slow thinking. But today it's one of the main things shaping how these systems are actually built.

r001.rationale: The response says control needs reliable tens-to-hundreds-of-hertz updates and that cloud offloading adds latency jitter that is unacceptable for safety-critical behavior.

r002.rationale: The response discusses large models and onboard compute demands but does not mention diffusion-based inference or repeated network evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people underestimate is how different the constraints are once you leave the data center and put the model on a legged robot or a humanoid. When we train locomotion policies, those are tiny networks, a few layers of MLP, and they run at fifty hertz or more on a very modest onboard computer with no trouble. The moment you move to a vision-language-action model, you're talking about billions of parameters, and you want it to consume camera images, maybe multiple cameras, and produce actions in a tight loop. On a Jetson-class device, you're looking at something like a few hertz at best, and that's before you account for everything else that needs to share that compute, like state estimation, mapping, safety monitors.

And latency really matters for these systems in a way it doesn't for a chatbot. If a robot is walking and manipulating at the same time, a two or three hundred millisecond delay between seeing something and reacting to it is the difference between a smooth motion and knocking the object over, or in the worst case, falling. So the common workaround right now is a hierarchy, where the big model runs slowly and outputs something like a goal or a short action chunk, and a small fast policy fills in the gaps. That works, but it also means the large model is kind of blind to the fast dynamics, and you lose a lot of the reactivity you'd want.

The other piece is power and thermals. A humanoid has a battery budget, and if you're burning a couple hundred watts just on inference, that eats directly into runtime and into how much headroom you have for the actuators. You can offload to the cloud, but then you're dependent on connectivity and you add even more latency, which is not acceptable for anything safety-critical.

So the way I see it, the algorithms are kind of ahead of the hardware at the moment. We can show impressive demos with a tethered workstation or a very permissive setup, but making the same thing run fully onboard, at the rates that physical interaction demands, with the energy budget a real robot has, is still a genuinely hard engineering problem. That's why there's so much interest in distillation, in quantization, in smaller specialized models, and frankly in better edge accelerators. I think that gap will close, but today it's one of the main things standing between the demos and robots that are actually useful in the field.

r001.rationale: The response says cloud offloading adds latency and depends on connectivity, making it unacceptable for safety-critical tasks with tight reaction times.

r002.rationale: It discusses VLA model size and compute demand but does not mention diffusion-based inference or repeated network evaluations.

astra-6.text:
The challenge is that the model has to run on a robot with a very constrained compute budget. You don’t have the same power and cooling that you have in a data center, and you’re sharing that compute with perception, state estimation, and control.

With a vision-language-action model, you’re processing images and running a fairly large network to produce actions. It’s not enough to get a good answer eventually—you need the next action quickly enough to react to what’s happening. If inference takes too long, the world has already changed by the time you execute it.

You can move some of that computation off the robot, but then communication latency and reliability become part of your control loop. So the question is how much of that model’s capability we can fit onboard while still running fast enough to be useful.

r001.rationale: The response says offboard computation adds latency and reliability concerns to the control loop, but does not clearly state that those concerns make offboard execution impractical; it says some computation can be moved off the robot.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention diffusion-based inference or repeated network evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that the robot has to carry its compute with it. With a language model in a data center, you can add more GPUs. On a robot, you have constraints on power, weight, heat, and how much space you have available. And that compute also has to run perception, state estimation, and control—not just the vision-language-action model.

At the same time, robotics is very sensitive to latency. You’re not just waiting for an answer to a question; the world keeps moving while the model is thinking. If inference takes too long, the action can already be out of date by the time you execute it. Sending everything to the cloud introduces additional latency and dependence on connectivity.

So the question isn’t only whether a big model can produce the right action. It’s whether it can produce that action reliably, fast enough, on the hardware you can actually put on the robot. That makes smaller models and approaches that separate slower, high-level reasoning from fast, low-level control particularly interesting.

r001.rationale: The response explains that robotics requires fast inference because the world keeps moving, and that cloud execution adds latency and connectivity dependence, making offboard execution unsuitable.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention diffusion-based VLA inference or repeated network evaluations as a source of computational demand.
